This is ungraded practice. It collects the lab of Session 30 into one short study that you can use to check your understanding: encode the rule, update the row synchronously, build a space-time diagram, and compare outcomes across experiments [@wolfram1983statistical].

You can follow the guide here:

[1D Cellular Automata](cellular-1d.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Rule Exploration](rule-exploration.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Boundary Conditions](ca-boundary-conditions.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Game of Life](game-of-life.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Goals

The practice checks three skills:

- Translate a rule number into a working local update.
- Simulate repeated synchronous updates on a one-dimensional lattice.
- Interpret how rule choice, initial condition and boundary shape the global pattern.

## Core tasks

1. Implement `apply_rule()` and a reusable `simulate_ca()` function.
2. Reproduce a space-time diagram for Rule 30 starting from a single occupied cell at the centre.
3. Compare at least three rules from the set `{30, 90, 110, 184}` using the same initial condition.
4. For one chosen rule, compare two different initial conditions, one single-seed row and one random row.
5. Write a short paragraph that explains which features are controlled by the rule and which depend strongly on the initial condition.

## Questions to answer

- Which rule in your experiments produced the most regular pattern?
- Which rule was most sensitive to the initial condition? Support your answer with the Hamming distance after a single flip.
- Did you find one rule that already looks like transport or directed motion? Explain why.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Optional extensions

- Implement periodic boundary conditions and compare the result with fixed-zero edges.
- Add a stochastic flip rule, for example flipping a cell with small probability after each update.
- Track the density of occupied cells over time for one rule and interpret the trend.
- Add interactivity to the initial row, either in a notebook or with the reference script.
- Find a Game of Life pattern of at most 5 cells that grows for more than 100 generations before it settles.
:::

## Tips

- Test `apply_rule()` on a short row before you run a long simulation.
- Print the rule table once so you know which output corresponds to each neighbourhood.
- Keep the first experiments small enough that you can inspect the pattern visually.
- Reuse the same plotting code when you compare rules so the differences are easier to see.

Reference code: [amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py](../../amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py), [amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py](../../amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py) and [amlab/cellular_automata/life.py](../../amlab/cellular_automata/life.py).

## Exit question

On a ring of 100 cells, you run Rule 30 for 1000 steps and see no repetition. A classmate concludes that Rule 30 is aperiodic on this ring. Is the conclusion correct?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. A ring of 100 cells has $2^{100}$ configurations, so every orbit is eventually periodic. The period can be far longer than 1000 steps, which is why you see no repetition. What you observe is a long transient or a long cycle of a finite system, not true aperiodicity.
:::
